title: OT/ICS Threat Intel - Marine
description: Curated OT/ICS cybersecurity advisories, incidents and threat intelligence from primary sources. Editorial summaries by Mike Holcomb in partnership with UtilSec.

_otthreatfeed.usage: Free to reuse with attribution. Credit 'Mike Holcomb & UtilSec' and link back to otthreatfeed.com and to each item's linked primary source. Summaries are editorial paraphrase - verify against the primary source before acting.

items.title: September’s ICS patch wave lands on the controllers and relays behind terminal power, cranes and shore systems
items.content_text: Schneider Electric and Siemens shipped their September fixes on 8 September, and two items reach directly into port and vessel estates. Schneider’s most severe is an authentication flaw in the Modicon M580 and M580 Safety controllers, CVE-2026-3869 at CVSS 9.2 — the M580 family runs conveyor lines, bulk handling, pump rooms and shore-power switching at terminals across the sector. Alongside it are high-severity fixes for the PowerLogic T300 RTU, formerly Easergy T300, and EcoStruxure IT Data Center Expert, plus a medium-severity SCADAPack x70 defect. Siemens issued nine advisories, seven of them on 8 September, headlined by fourteen CVEs in Reyrolle 7SR5 protection relays where a session-identifier leak allows authentication bypass. Aveva patched four flaws in the PIMBoards component of Pipeline Integrity Monitor, including a hardcoded encryption key. None is reported as exploited.

_otthreatfeed.category: Top Story
_otthreatfeed.source_name: Schneider Electric and Siemens ProductCERT September security advisories (incl. SSA-142885) — round-up via SecurityWeek
_otthreatfeed.date_note: Vendor advisories published 8 Sep 2026

items.title: FBI seizes the Chinese scanning and relay platforms built out of other people’s routers and IoT devices
items.content_text: The Justice Department and FBI announced court-authorised seizures on 26 August of two linked platforms, QScan and QTRouter, operated by a PRC state-sponsored group the government calls QTFY and tied to a Nanjing contractor. QScan handled reconnaissance against US critical infrastructure; QTRouter relayed the resulting intrusions through compromised third-party routers and IoT devices so the traffic arrived from ordinary domestic addresses. Both platforms are now inoperable because the seized domains were hard-coded into the malware. For ports, terminals and fleet operators the relay design is the part worth absorbing: the small, unmanaged, internet-connected devices that fill a maritime estate — VSAT routers, gate cameras, crane telemetry gateways, remote-monitoring boxes — are exactly the population these platforms recruited, and source addresses proved nothing.

_otthreatfeed.category: Incident — State-sponsored reconnaissance infrastructure seized
_otthreatfeed.source_name: US Department of Justice press release and unsealed court documents — corroborated by TechCrunch and UPI
_otthreatfeed.date_note: Seizures announced and confirmed 26 Aug 2026; described activity dates from at least 2018 to 2026

items.title: A CEVA Logistics breach reached European warehouses and spilled customer data through the retail chain
items.content_text: CEVA Logistics disclosed a breach affecting European warehouse operations, with customer data exposed through the retail clients it serves. Third-party logistics sits between the terminal and the consignee and holds the data that describes what is moving, for whom and when — booking references, consignee details, delivery schedules and, in some arrangements, the credentials used to update port and carrier systems. For a terminal operator or shipping line the exposure is indirect but material: an attacker who holds a logistics provider’s booking data has a very effective basis for social engineering against your gate, your documentation team and your customer service desk.

items.title: A state administration refused to pay and its infrastructure vulnerability analyses were published
items.content_text: Rhysida released data taken from Berlin’s state administration on 4 September after the city declined a demand reported at 30 bitcoin. The claimed set is around 5.79 TB across roughly 1.44 million files and, alongside personnel and payroll records, is reported to include vulnerability analyses of the city’s water supply and plaintext credentials for municipal systems including a building atlas, a payments database and administrator accounts. Berlin’s account has data leaving from 7 August through around 12 August, with affected departments not physically disconnected until 14 August. Most US port authorities are public bodies subject to the same dynamics: the facility security assessment, the new MTSA cyber assessment, terminal drawings and crane and gate system documentation frequently sit on a state or municipal network run by someone other than the port’s own security team.
tags: Incident — Public-authority breach publishes infrastructure risk documentation

items.title: Treasury names an Iranian intelligence-directed hacking network in an action that also covers vessels
items.content_text: The US Treasury designated an Iranian Ministry of Intelligence and Security-directed hacking network on 24 August as part of a wider action covering nearly 60 Iran-linked people, entities and vessels, with a related State Department reward notice. Treasury states the network has breached and exfiltrated data from US energy companies, defence contractors, healthcare providers, IT firms and banks since at least late 2023. The maritime relevance runs on two tracks. The cyber designation describes espionage rather than manipulation of ship or terminal systems. The vessel designations are a sanctions-compliance matter that lands on your screening process and your charterers, and the two arrive in the same document without being the same problem.
tags: Incident — Sanctions action touching maritime entities

items.title: Google says a criminal group ran an entire credential-harvesting campaign with autonomous agents in under six hours
items.content_text: Google’s Threat Intelligence Group reported on 8 September that a financially motivated actor executed a large-scale credential-harvesting campaign end to end in less than six hours using an autonomous multi-agent framework — the agents, not operators, carried the campaign through its stages. GTIG separately observed actors going after proprietary AI models across healthcare, government and media, stealing API credentials and running unauthorised AI workloads inside victims’ own cloud tenants. Its assessment is blunt: assume every threat actor is using AI to some degree. For ports, terminals and vessel operators the practical consequence is timing. Credential phishing against shoreside schedulers, agents, chandlers and crewing staff is the standard first move against a maritime estate, and a six-hour campaign lands entirely inside a single watch — often one with satellite latency and no responder aboard.
tags: Threat Intel — Autonomous multi-agent intrusion tooling

_otthreatfeed.category: Threat Intel — Autonomous multi-agent intrusion tooling
_otthreatfeed.source_name: Google Threat Intelligence Group reporting — via The Hacker News
_otthreatfeed.date_note: Published 8 Sep 2026

items.title: Fire Ant turns routers and authentication servers into listening posts inside critical-infrastructure networks
items.content_text: Sygnia published research on 30 August showing the China-nexus group it tracks as Fire Ant has moved beyond VMware hypervisors into network infrastructure itself: Cisco IOS XR routers, TACACS authentication servers and Linux management hosts inside a large interconnected estate. Router implants suppressed chosen syslog messages, opened outbound sessions and offered interactive shells that logged nothing; on TACACS the actor hooked the running daemon and copied administrator credentials as logins were approved. Sygnia observed scanning and connection attempts toward linked critical-infrastructure networks, without confirming compromise there. Ports and terminals should read this as a warning about the layer they examine least. Terminal operating systems, crane and gate networks and shore-to-ship links all traverse routers a third party maintains — and the audit trail a Coast Guard incident report would rest on comes from those same devices.
tags: Threat Intel — State-nexus compromise of network and authentication infrastructure

_otthreatfeed.category: Threat Intel — State-nexus compromise of network and authentication infrastructure

items.title: Eighteen frontier models were run at a real enterprise network — one completed the whole kill chain unaided
items.content_text: Booz Allen published its Cyber Weapon Index and an accompanying report on 4 September, grading eighteen frontier AI models on how much of an intrusion they can carry out without a human driving. The models were run against a representative enterprise network rather than a benchmark; the top performer completed the full sequence — reconnaissance, initial access, lateral movement and objective — unaided, while most managed individual stages. The authors’ conclusion is about time rather than novelty: nothing in the tested behaviour was a new technique, but the interval between a foothold and a consequence compresses when the attacker never pauses to think. Booz Allen also reports that defensive playbooks written specifically against autonomous attackers cut their success rate by more than 95% in the same tests. For a terminal or fleet operator this lands on the response side: shore-side monitoring is often business-hours, and a vessel in passage has satellite latency and no local responder at all.
tags: Research — measured autonomous attack capability in frontier AI models; no incident

_otthreatfeed.category: Research — measured autonomous attack capability in frontier AI models; no incident
_otthreatfeed.source_name: Booz Allen Cyber Weapon Index and the report “The Offensive Frontier: AI as the Attacker”, reported by Industrial Cyber — vendor-published research; the figures are the authors’ own test results and have not been independently reproduced
_otthreatfeed.date_note: Published and reported 4 Sep 2026 — verified 6 Sep 2026

items.title: Six steps to being able to disconnect the terminal — and a three-month planning horizon
items.content_text: Nozomi Networks published a practitioner summary on 2 September of the Five Eyes “CI Fortify” guidance released in late July, reducing it to six steps: identify vital systems and their dependencies; establish trust levels and connection maps; pre-build the separation points; create and test graduated isolation plans; retain visibility while isolated; and run post-isolation checks before reconnecting. For a terminal the hard step is the first one, because the dependency map runs outside the fence — customs and manifest feeds, carrier systems, the terminal operating system’s cloud components. North Carolina Ports demonstrated the graduated version in August by moving cargo processing to manual while vessel work continued. Nozomi’s planning horizon of up to three months of isolated operation is the part worth testing against your own manual fallbacks, which are usually scoped for days.

_otthreatfeed.category: Research — Isolation readiness, practitioner guidance
_otthreatfeed.source_name: Nozomi Networks Labs analysis of the CISA / ASD ACSC / NCSC-UK / CCCS “CI Fortify” guidance
_otthreatfeed.date_note: Analysis published 2 Sep 2026; underlying guidance published 28 Jul 2026

items.title: AI-assisted exploit porting: a working PLC exploit moved to a second controller model in hours
items.content_text: Forescout’s Vedere Labs set a large language model the task of taking a working remote-code-execution exploit for one WAGO controller — the 750-852, via CVE-2021-31886, a pre-authentication buffer overflow in its Nucleus FTP server — and re-targeting it at a related model, the 750-831. It worked, but not cheaply or unattended: the final stage alone ran more than eight hours and over $500 in API costs, with a researcher steering throughout. A later session aimed at building a command-and-control implant wrote a payload into flash-mapped memory and permanently bricked the test controller. For terminals and vessels the point is portability. Cargo handling, ballast and power-management controllers come in close model families, and an exploit proven on one variant is now cheaper to move to its siblings than most risk registers assume.
tags: Research — AI-assisted exploit porting against PLCs

_otthreatfeed.category: Research — AI-assisted exploit porting against PLCs

items.title: NCSC issues an alert: increased targeting of OT across multiple sectors globally, and it has already caused real-world disruption
items.content_text: The NCSC published a formal alert on 27 August stating it has seen increased targeting of operational technology across multiple sectors globally, including in the UK, by a range of threat actors, with some limited real-world disruption already resulting. It names no victims, actors or techniques. For ports, terminals and shipowners the relevant line is the one about assumption: the NCSC tells organisations not to believe their OT is unreachable from the internet without verifying it, because exposure comes from misconfiguration, legacy connections and unmanaged assets. Maritime OT is unusually good at generating all three — crane and straddle-carrier control systems commissioned by an OEM and still reachable over a vendor support link, terminal operating system interfaces, shore-power and bunkering controls, and vessel systems whose remote maintenance path was set up for a class survey and never withdrawn. The alert also maps closely onto IACS UR E26 and E27 expectations already binding on newbuilds.
tags: Threat Intelligence — National agency alert on OT targeting

items.title: Baltic GNSS interference is a coordinated transmitter network, not scattered jamming
items.content_text: Analysis of Baltic GNSS interference published this month characterises the activity as a coordinated network of transmitters rather than opportunistic local jamming, with consistent geographic patterns and sustained operation. That framing changes the planning assumption for a bridge team: interference in these waters is a persistent environmental condition to be navigated around, not an intermittent fault to be reported and waited out. The wider picture supports it — maritime GNSS interference reached record levels earlier this year, and a single 24-hour period in the Arabian Gulf reportedly affected more than 1,100 vessels with degraded AIS data and elevated collision risk. Position, navigation and timing loss also propagates into timestamping, ECDIS and some engine-monitoring systems.
tags: Threat intel — Coordinated GNSS interference affecting navigation

_otthreatfeed.category: Threat intel — Coordinated GNSS interference affecting navigation

items.title: CISA’s red team took a domain undetected — the tooling was fine, the monitoring was not
items.content_text: CISA advisory AA26-237A publishes paired red-team results from a water and wastewater entity and a government organisation, run with comparable tradecraft. One organisation detected and responded; the other did not notice a domain compromise. The advisory is direct about the reason, and it is not product spend: both had capable tooling, but only one had someone reviewing the output, correlating identity events and practising the response. Port authorities and shipping lines recognise the shape of this immediately, because terminal operating systems, gate systems and corporate IT frequently share one Active Directory, and monitoring is often outsourced to a provider whose alerting nobody has tested.
tags: Threat intel — Federal red-team assessment findings

items.title: 1,140 industrial ransomware victims in a quarter, and none of them needed the control system touched
items.content_text: Dragos counted 1,140 ransomware incidents at industrial organisations in the second quarter of 2026, up roughly 12 percent on the first, and made the point that operators do not need control-system access to stop work. The maritime version of that argument is short: nobody needs to touch a crane PLC to close a terminal. Encrypting the terminal operating system, the gate system, the billing platform or the documentation estate produces the same result, which is exactly what North Carolina Ports demonstrated this month when it moved to manual gate processing. Those systems rarely receive the segmentation and restoration attention that crane and yard automation does.
tags: Threat intel — Quarterly industrial ransomware analysis

items.title: A CVSS 10 pre-auth flaw in the RMM platform your terminal’s IT provider runs — N-able N-central leads CISA’s 8 September KEV batch
items.content_text: CISA added four actively exploited vulnerabilities to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on 8 September. The one that matters most to ports and terminals is CVE-2026-86218 in N-able N-central, a static code injection flaw scored CVSS 10.0 that gives pre-authentication remote code execution. N-able confirmed exploitation in the wild; Huntress reported attacks against N-central’s API and appliance logs from 4 September, and N-able shipped 2026.3 Hotfix 4 on 5 September — its fourth hotfix in five weeks. N-central is a remote monitoring and management platform, which means an agent with system-level rights on managed endpoints. Many terminals, port authorities and smaller vessel-management companies outsource shoreside IT to an MSP running exactly this kind of console. Also added: two Windows zero-days granting SYSTEM (CVE-2026-81963, CVE-2026-85880) and an Adobe Commerce template-injection flaw at CVSS 10.0. The federal remediation deadline is 11 September.

_otthreatfeed.category: Critical Advisory — Actively exploited, KEV-listed
_otthreatfeed.source_name: CISA Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog addition of 8 Sep 2026, with N-able and Huntress reporting — corroborated by BleepingComputer and SecurityWeek
_otthreatfeed.date_note: Added to KEV 8 Sep 2026; vendor hotfix released 5 Sep 2026

items.title: CISA’s 3 September batch reaches vendor remote access and the firmware tool — IXON VPN client, Rockwell ControlFLASH, Ignition
items.content_text: CISA published a further set of ICS advisories on 3 September. Three matter for terminals and vessel operators. ICSA-26-246-02 covers the IXON VPN Client, where CVE-2026-75925 allows remote code execution with elevated privileges on the machine running the client in versions before 1.4.7 — the pattern behind most crane, gate and terminal-automation support contracts. ICSA-26-246-03 covers Rockwell Automation ControlFLASH at V15.07 and earlier, where CVE-2026-12663 lets commands or code run at the logged-in user’s permission level; ControlFLASH is the firmware tool for the controllers behind ship-to-shore cranes, conveyors and shore-power systems. ICSA-26-246-06 covers Inductive Automation Ignition, where any authenticated user can create projects — Ignition turns up as the visualisation layer in terminal operating environments. None is reported as exploited.
tags: Critical Advisory — Remote-access client, firmware tool and SCADA platform

_otthreatfeed.category: Critical Advisory — Remote-access client, firmware tool and SCADA platform
_otthreatfeed.source_name: CISA ICS advisories ICSA-26-246-02 (IXON VPN Client), ICSA-26-246-03 (Rockwell Automation ControlFLASH) and ICSA-26-246-06 (Inductive Automation Ignition)
_otthreatfeed.date_note: Published 3 Sep 2026

items.title: A CVSS 10 pre-auth flaw in SonicWall’s SMA1000 remote-access gateway is being exploited, and CISA gave agencies three days
items.content_text: SonicWall disclosed on 1 September that two previously unknown vulnerabilities in its SMA1000 secure remote access gateway and SSL-VPN appliance are being exploited in the wild; the company says it found both the flaws and the exploitation internally. CVE-2026-83548, scored CVSS 10, is a pre-authentication server-side request forgery in the Appliance Work Place interface. CVE-2026-83549, at 7.8, is an operating-system command injection flaw in the Appliance Management Console. Chained, the pair gives an unauthenticated attacker remote code execution on the appliance itself. CISA added both to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on 2 September with a 5 September deadline for federal civilian agencies, and marked both entries as requiring forensic triage under Binding Operational Directive 26-04 — a signal that patching alone does not close the incident. Affected models are the SMA1000 6210, 7210 and 8200v; SSL-VPN running on SonicWall firewalls and the SMA 100 series are not affected.

_otthreatfeed.category: Critical Advisory — Actively exploited, KEV-listed
_otthreatfeed.source_name: SonicWall PSIRT advisory and the CISA Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog addition of 2 Sep 2026 — corroborated by SecurityWeek, BleepingComputer, Help Net Security and Sophos
_otthreatfeed.date_note: Vendor advisory published 1 Sep 2026; added to CISA KEV 2 Sep 2026 — verified 3 Sep 2026

items.title: A print server chained to unauthenticated code execution — PaperCut’s zero-day pair lands in KEV
items.content_text: PaperCut confirmed on 27 August that it was investigating active exploitation of its NG and MF print-management products, and assigned CVE-2026-81578 and CVE-2026-82078 the following day. The first lets an unauthenticated attacker reach the Application Server and change its configuration; the second turns that change into arbitrary code execution through unsafe reflection. Chained, they give a network-adjacent attacker code execution with no credentials at all, and CISA added both to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on 31 August. Print management almost never appears on an OT asset register. The server usually does hold a domain service account, does sit on the same segment as engineering workstations, and is reachable from nearly every host in the estate — which makes it a convenient staging point rather than a target in its own right. Arctic Wolf reported on 6 September that it is seeing the chain used in practice: after gaining execution, operators run reconnaissance, create privileged accounts and harvest credentials and PaperCut configuration secrets — behaviour consistent with establishing a durable foothold rather than a smash-and-grab.

_otthreatfeed.category: Critical Advisory — Actively exploited, KEV-listed
_otthreatfeed.source_name: CISA Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog addition and the PaperCut security bulletin — corroborated by SecurityWeek, Help Net Security, Rapid7 and The Hacker News
_otthreatfeed.date_note: Vendor disclosed active exploitation 27 Aug 2026; CVEs assigned 28 Aug 2026; added to KEV 31 Aug 2026; post-exploitation activity reported by Arctic Wolf 6 Sep 2026; verified 7 Sep 2026

items.title: Three more exploited flaws land in KEV — a Linux kernel bug, a JFrog Artifactory path traversal and a two-year-old ownCloud authentication bypass
items.content_text: CISA added three more actively exploited flaws to the KEV catalogue on 27 August, a day after the six-flaw batch that included NetScaler. None is a marine product, and that is precisely why they matter here: port and vessel OT rides on ordinary IT. CVE-2026-53362 is a Linux kernel flaw, and the terminal operating system server, gate OCR appliance, network sensor and many bridge and engine-room gateways are Linux underneath — often as vendor appliances patched on the supplier’s timetable, not yours. CVE-2026-66384 is a path traversal in JFrog Artifactory, relevant wherever firmware or software builds for shipboard or terminal equipment are staged. CVE-2023-49105 is an ownCloud authentication bypass patched since late 2023; the instances still exposed are usually ones nobody owns. The North Carolina Ports outage earlier this month is a reminder of how quickly an IT-layer compromise becomes manual gate processing.

items.title: Hard-coded credentials in a Class B AIS transponder that stopped being supported six years ago
items.content_text: CISA advisory ICSA-26-237-07 covers the FURUNO FA-50 Class B AIS transponder, in all versions. The device uses hard-coded credentials, and some settings can be changed on the management screen without authentication, so an attacker with those credentials and access to the in-vessel network can alter device configuration. Production ended in October 2020 and FURUNO has confirmed no further software updates will be provided; the vendor’s recommendation is to keep the unit off the internet and control physical access to the vessel. This is a small-vessel and workboat problem more than a deep-sea one, and the risk it creates is to the accuracy of the AIS picture other vessels rely on.
tags: Advisory — Shipboard AIS transponder, end of support

items.title: The NetScaler flaw is now confirmed exploited and in KEV — federal deadline 29 August
items.content_text: CISA added CVE-2026-8452 to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalogue on 26 August, moving the Citrix NetScaler ADC and Gateway issue to confirmed exploitation in the wild. It is a heap overflow in SAML single sign-on parsing, rated CVSS 8.8, needing no authentication, and reachable when the appliance is configured as a Gateway or AAA virtual server. Canada’s Cyber Centre reported indications of exploitation from around 17 August after a public proof of concept. In maritime organisations NetScaler commonly fronts the remote access used by shoreside staff, crewing and technical departments, and by the OEMs who support engine, cargo and automation systems on vessels. Exploitation has not tailed off: reporting on 5 September describes continued attempts against the authentication bypass from multiple geolocations, so an appliance patched late should be treated as possibly already touched rather than simply late.

items.title: CVSS 10.0 on a Siemens edge gateway that is dual-homed by design
items.content_text: Siemens’ August advisory set includes a maximum-severity missing-authentication flaw in SIMATIC IoT2050 Advanced devices, allowing a remote unauthenticated attacker to execute code with elevated privileges. Ten Siemens advisories landed in the same batch alongside Schneider Electric and Phoenix Contact publications. The maritime relevance is placement rather than score: edge gateways of this class are deployed precisely to move data from crane, yard, reefer or shipboard automation networks out to a monitoring platform or an OEM cloud service, which makes them dual-homed by design and frequently the one device with a route in both directions.
tags: Advisory — Maximum severity, Siemens edge gateway

items.title: 117 federal incident-reporting rules across 27 agencies — and a maritime operator can be inside several of them at once
items.content_text: The McCrary Institute and the US Chamber of Commerce published analysis on 8 September, drawing on GAO work, counting 117 federal cyber incident reporting regulations spread across 27 agencies, 48 of which apply to private industry. Their argument is operational rather than political: duplicative filings with different thresholds, formats and clocks pull the same handful of people off containment during the first hours of an incident. Maritime is a clear example of the overlap. A single event at a US-flagged vessel or an MTSA-regulated facility can trigger reporting to the National Response Center under 33 CFR 101 Subpart F, a Coast Guard Captain of the Port notification, and, once CIRCIA rules are finalised — expected this autumn — a separate CISA filing, on top of any flag-state, class or charterer obligation.

_otthreatfeed.category: Regulation & Policy — Incident reporting burden
_otthreatfeed.source_name: McCrary Institute and US Chamber of Commerce analysis citing GAO findings — via Industrial Cyber
_otthreatfeed.date_note: Published 8 Sep 2026; CIRCIA final rule expected autumn 2026

items.title: CISA and the G7 tell operators to start the post-quantum inventory now — the deadline is set by your asset lifetimes, not by them
items.content_text: CISA and the G7 Cyber Security Working Group issued a joint call on 4 September for governments and organisations to begin the transition to post-quantum cryptography, setting out a phased, risk-based approach: inventory the cryptography in use and the dependencies that carry it, identify the data and systems whose exposure would outlast the migration, and hold a written transition plan rather than a procurement wish. The statement is explicit about store-now-decrypt-later — traffic captured today can be decrypted later — and about the second-order problem, which is that authentication and firmware-signing chains rest on the same public-key algorithms. It is guidance, not a rule, and no deadline attaches. The relevance to maritime is asset lifetime: a vessel or terminal control system commissioned now will still be running in the 2040s, and the cryptography inside its firmware-signing and remote-access chains is being chosen today.
tags: Guidance — CISA and G7 joint call to begin the post-quantum cryptography transition; no deadline attached

_otthreatfeed.category: Guidance — CISA and G7 joint call to begin the post-quantum cryptography transition; no deadline attached
_otthreatfeed.source_name: Joint statement from CISA and the G7 Cyber Security Working Group, reported by Industrial Cyber
_otthreatfeed.date_note: Published and reported 4 Sep 2026 — verified 6 Sep 2026

items.title: OpenAI pledges $1bn of subsidised AI defence for critical-infrastructure operators — terms not yet published
items.content_text: OpenAI said on 4 September that it will commit $1 billion to an initiative it calls Daybreak, offering subsidised AI cyber capabilities, training and technical assistance to defenders of critical infrastructure. Cost, eligibility and what “subsidised” means in practice have not been published, and no delivery timeline has been given. For ports, terminals and shipping lines the relevance is indirect but real: maritime security spending is usually set against a compliance calendar rather than a threat one, and subsidised capability changes what a mid-sized terminal operator can put in front of a terminal operating system without first winning a business case. Note it, wait for the eligibility terms, and when they arrive read them as you would any third-party arrangement touching vessel or terminal operational data — the Coast Guard’s new policy office is likely to have a view on where that data sits.

_otthreatfeed.category: Regulation & Policy — Industry initiative
_otthreatfeed.source_name: SecurityWeek reporting on OpenAI’s Daybreak announcement
_otthreatfeed.date_note: Announced and reported 4 Sep 2026

items.title: Six agencies publish outage-communication guidance for IT and OT service providers — and terminals sit on both sides of it
items.content_text: On 2 September the Canadian Centre for Cyber Security joined CISA, Australia’s ASD ACSC, NCSC-NZ, NCSC-UK and the FBI to publish joint guidance on communicating during IT and OT service outages, titled “Communicating Under Pressure: Best Practices for Service Providers.” It calls for a written incident communications plan with defined trigger thresholds and named audiences, plain-language updates, root-cause and technical detail end users can act on, and messaging aligned with legal and regulatory duties. Maritime is a good test case: when North Carolina Ports moved to manual cargo processing in early August, the operational question for every carrier, drayage firm and shipper on the other side was simply what to expect and for how long. A terminal is a service provider to that chain, and the guidance is written for exactly that position.

items.title: Britain moves to bar designated high-risk suppliers from critical infrastructure — without naming them publicly
items.content_text: The UK government has tabled late amendments to the Cyber Security and Resilience Bill that would let ministers stop critical-sector organisations from using technology suppliers designated as high risk. The Bill, introduced in November 2025 and now near the end of its passage through the Lords, already extends duties to energy, water, transport and health operators and pulls managed service providers, data centres and digital infrastructure into scope. The amendments were tabled on 24 August and reported on 2 September; they follow reporting that a small UK generating station ran manually for four days after a cyberattack. Designations would not necessarily be made public, which is the detail operators should notice: a supplier could be designated without a public list to check against, so the obligation to know your own supply chain moves from good practice to compliance exposure. None of this is in force yet, and the Bill has not completed its passage.

items.title: The Coast Guard now has one office that owns maritime cyber policy — expect the inspections to sharpen
items.content_text: The US Coast Guard has stood up the Office of Maritime Cybersecurity Policy (CG-MCP) as the central authority for cybersecurity policy covering ports, vessels and facilities across the Marine Transportation System, reporting to the Director of Inspections and Compliance. Its remit is to write policy, run a unified compliance strategy, coordinate enforcement and industry engagement, and track emerging technology and cyber risk. The move follows Government Accountability Office findings about gaps in Coast Guard cyber oversight. Nothing in the MTS cyber rule changes today, but the practical effect of consolidating policy and compliance under one office is usually consistency: the same questions, asked the same way, at more facilities.

items.title: Coast Guard cyber rule: training already required, Cybersecurity Plans due 16 July 2027
items.content_text: The Coast Guard’s cybersecurity rule for the Maritime Transportation System is in its phased implementation period. Annual cybersecurity training for personnel is already a requirement, and the Cybersecurity Plan submission deadline for covered US-flagged vessels, facilities and outer continental shelf facilities falls on 16 July 2027. The plan is not a paperwork exercise: it requires a named Cybersecurity Officer, an account of cyber risks to operational technology as well as information technology, defined incident response, and evidence of drills and exercises. The organisations that struggle are consistently the ones that start by writing the document rather than by producing the asset inventory the document has to describe.
